block3.title: Menyusun Laporan Transportasi
block3.text:
Many readers judge a long report by its headings, but a good heading does more than label a section. It gives the gist of the paragraph beneath it. When the heading is clear, a reader can skim the document and understand its scope in a few minutes.

The first chapter of a typical planning report usually sets the scope of the study. It explains which areas are included and which are excluded. Writers often add a short summary at the end of the chapter, so that readers can check the main findings before they move on. Each paragraph in that summary should match the heading above it, otherwise the reader may feel misled.

The second section describes the arrangement of bus routes in the city. Routes are grouped by district, and each group has its own subheading. This order makes it easier to compare routes that serve similar neighbourhoods. The logic of the arrangement is explained in the opening sentences, so the reader knows what to expect.

A smooth flow of ideas is just as important as a clear heading. If a paragraph jumps from cost to design without a link, the reader loses the thread. Good writers use linking phrases to keep the flow natural, such as 'as a result' or 'in contrast'. These phrases tell the reader how each idea connects to the one before it.

The final section returns to the purpose of the report. It reviews the three options and recommends the one with the best balance of cost and coverage. The recommendation is written in plain language, so that councillors can act on it without reading the technical appendix. The summary at the end repeats the key figures in one table.

Finally, the report includes a list of references and a short glossary. These parts are not part of the main argument, but they help the reader verify the figures. A careful reader should check whether each claim has a source, because a report without sources is difficult to trust. Many readers also compare the figures in the glossary with the main text, since a single paragraph can change the meaning of a whole table. Writers usually begin with a rough draft, which they revise before the final version.
